question: Under General Obligations Law Section 7-108, enacted as part of the Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act (HSTPA) of 2019, a residential landlord subject to the section may generally demand a security deposit or advance of no more than:
choice_a: Two months' rent
choice_b: One month's rent
choice_c: One and a half months' rent
choice_d: There is no statutory cap on the deposit amount
explanation: GOL 7-108(1-a), added by the HSTPA in 2019, caps a security deposit or advance at one month's rent for most residential dwelling units, with narrow exceptions such as certain seasonal rentals and owner-occupied cooperative units.
source_note: NY source: General Obligations Law Section 7-108(1-a) (HSTPA 2019) -- security deposit cap of one month's rent

question: Under GOL 7-108 (HSTPA 2019), after a tenant vacates a rental unit, the landlord must provide the tenant with an itemized statement of any deductions from the security deposit and return the balance within:
choice_a: Thirty days after the tenant has vacated
choice_b: Forty-five days after the tenant has vacated
choice_c: Fourteen days after the tenant has vacated
choice_d: Sixty days after the tenant has vacated
explanation: GOL 7-108(2)(a) requires the landlord to provide a written, itemized statement of deductions and return the remaining deposit balance to the tenant within fourteen days after the tenant has vacated the premises.
source_note: NY source: General Obligations Law Section 7-108(2)(a) (HSTPA 2019) -- 14-day itemized statement/return deadline

question: Under GOL 7-108 (HSTPA 2019), a landlord who fails to provide the tenant with the required itemized statement of security deposit deductions within the statutory deadline after the tenant vacates:
choice_a: May still retain up to half the deposit without documentation
choice_b: Is granted an automatic 30-day extension to comply
choice_c: Faces no consequence as long as the deposit is eventually returned
choice_d: Forfeits the right to retain any portion of the deposit
explanation: GOL 7-108(2)(a) provides that a landlord who fails to timely provide the itemized statement forfeits the right to retain any portion of the deposit, even if the landlord could otherwise have justified deductions.
source_note: NY source: General Obligations Law Section 7-108(2)(a) (HSTPA 2019) -- forfeiture penalty for untimely itemized statement

question: Under GOL 7-108 (HSTPA 2019), when itemizing deductions from a tenant's security deposit, a landlord may charge for damage to the unit beyond normal use, but may NOT deduct for:
choice_a: Ordinary wear and tear
choice_b: Unpaid rent owed by the tenant
choice_c: Damage to the unit beyond normal wear and tear
choice_d: Nonpayment of utility charges the tenant was contractually obligated to pay
explanation: GOL 7-108 permits reasonable, itemized deductions for unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear, and certain unpaid utility charges the tenant owed, but expressly excludes ordinary wear and tear from chargeable deductions.
source_note: NY source: General Obligations Law Section 7-108 (HSTPA 2019) -- ordinary wear and tear excluded from deductions

question: Under GOL 7-108 (HSTPA 2019), before a tenant's occupancy begins, the landlord must offer the tenant the opportunity to:
choice_a: Select the paint color for the unit at the landlord's expense
choice_b: Inspect the premises and receive written documentation of its condition before move-in
choice_c: Negotiate the security deposit amount downward in exchange for a longer lease
choice_d: Waive all inspection rights in exchange for a reduced deposit
explanation: GOL 7-108 requires the landlord to offer the tenant a pre-occupancy inspection of the premises and to provide written documentation of the unit's condition, helping establish a baseline for later security deposit deduction disputes.
source_note: NY source: General Obligations Law Section 7-108 (HSTPA 2019) -- move-in inspection right

question: Under GOL 7-108 (HSTPA 2019), before a tenant moves out, the landlord must notify the tenant of the right to request a move-out inspection so that the tenant may:
choice_a: Automatically receive a full refund of the deposit regardless of any damage
choice_b: Demand the landlord waive the itemized statement requirement
choice_c: Be present for the inspection and have the opportunity to remedy any conditions identified before deductions are taken
choice_d: Require the landlord to repaint the unit before vacating
explanation: GOL 7-108 requires the landlord to notify the tenant of the right to be present at a move-out inspection, conducted with reasonable advance notice, so the tenant has an opportunity to address or remedy conditions before the landlord finalizes deposit deductions.
source_note: NY source: General Obligations Law Section 7-108 (HSTPA 2019) -- move-out inspection notice and cure opportunity

question: Under RPL Section 226-c, added by the HSTPA in 2019, a landlord who wishes to raise a residential tenant's rent by 5% or more, or who wishes to decline to renew the tenancy, must give the tenant AT LEAST how much advance written notice if the tenant has occupied the unit for less than one year?
choice_a: Sixty days
choice_b: Ninety days
choice_c: Fifteen days
choice_d: Thirty days
explanation: RPL 226-c requires at least 30 days' notice of a rent increase of 5% or more or of a lease non-renewal when the tenant's occupancy has been less than one year, with longer notice tiers for longer occupancy.
source_note: NY source: RPL 226-c (HSTPA 2019) -- 30-day notice tier for occupancy under one year

question: Under RPL 226-c (HSTPA 2019), a landlord seeking to raise rent 5% or more or decline to renew a tenancy must give the tenant AT LEAST sixty days' advance written notice when the tenant's occupancy has been:
choice_a: More than one year but less than two years
choice_b: Less than one year
choice_c: More than two years
choice_d: Exactly six months
explanation: RPL 226-c sets a 60-day notice requirement for a rent increase of 5% or more or a non-renewal where the tenant has occupied the unit for more than one year but less than two years.
source_note: NY source: RPL 226-c (HSTPA 2019) -- 60-day notice tier for occupancy of 1-2 years

question: Under RPL 226-c (HSTPA 2019), a landlord seeking to raise rent 5% or more or decline to renew a tenancy must give the tenant AT LEAST ninety days' advance written notice once the tenant's occupancy has continued for:
choice_a: More than six months
choice_b: More than two years
choice_c: Exactly one year
choice_d: More than one year but less than two years
explanation: RPL 226-c requires at least 90 days' notice of a 5%-or-greater rent increase or a non-renewal once the tenant has occupied the unit for more than two years -- the longest of the three statutory notice tiers.
source_note: NY source: RPL 226-c (HSTPA 2019) -- 90-day notice tier for occupancy over two years

question: Under RPL 226-c (HSTPA 2019), the tiered 30/60/90-day advance notice requirement applies to which TWO categories of landlord action toward a residential tenant?
choice_a: Any rent increase of any amount, and a change in the tenant's assigned parking space
choice_b: A change in the superintendent, and a rent increase of any amount
choice_c: A rent increase of 5% or more, and a decision not to renew the tenancy
choice_d: A decision to renew the tenancy, and a rent decrease of any amount
explanation: RPL 226-c's tiered notice requirement is triggered specifically by (1) a proposed rent increase of 5% or more over the current rent, or (2) a landlord's decision not to renew the tenancy -- not by rent increases under 5%, rent decreases, or unrelated changes.
source_note: NY source: RPL 226-c (HSTPA 2019) -- triggering events for tiered notice requirement

question: Under RPL 226-c (HSTPA 2019), if a landlord fails to provide the required advance notice of a rent increase of 5% or more or of a non-renewal, the effect is that:
choice_a: The tenant must vacate immediately regardless of the notice defect
choice_b: The rent increase takes effect anyway but is capped at 5%
choice_c: The landlord forfeits the right to ever raise the rent on that tenant
choice_d: The tenancy continues on the existing lease terms until the statutory notice period has run
explanation: RPL 226-c provides that if a landlord fails to give the required notice, the tenant's occupancy continues under the existing lease terms and rent until the full notice period has elapsed, notwithstanding any contrary lease provision.
source_note: NY source: RPL 226-c (HSTPA 2019) -- effect of landlord's failure to give timely notice

question: A tenant has occupied an apartment for two years and three months under successive one-year leases. The landlord now wants to raise the rent by 6% at the next renewal. Under RPL 226-c (HSTPA 2019), how much advance written notice must the landlord give?
choice_a: At least ninety days
choice_b: At least sixty days
choice_c: At least thirty days
choice_d: No advance notice is required because the tenant is on a lease, not month-to-month
explanation: Because the tenant's occupancy exceeds two years and the proposed increase (6%) is 5% or more, the 90-day notice tier under RPL 226-c applies; RPL 226-c's notice requirement applies to leased tenancies, not only month-to-month arrangements.
source_note: NY source: RPL 226-c (HSTPA 2019) -- applied scenario, occupancy over two years

question: Under RPL 226-c (HSTPA 2019), a tenant's length of occupancy for purposes of determining the applicable notice tier is measured by:
choice_a: Only the number of months remaining on the current lease term
choice_b: The cumulative time the tenant has occupied the unit, or the length of the tenancy under the current lease, whichever is longer
choice_c: Only the length of the very first lease term, ignoring any renewals
choice_d: The date the tenant's security deposit was originally paid, regardless of any gaps in occupancy
explanation: RPL 226-c measures occupancy length by the cumulative time the tenant has occupied the residence, or the length of the tenancy under each lease, whichever calculation yields the longer period -- protecting long-term tenants who have renewed multiple shorter leases.
source_note: NY source: RPL 226-c (HSTPA 2019) -- method for measuring occupancy length

question: Under RPL Section 238-a, added by the HSTPA in 2019, a residential landlord may charge a late fee for overdue rent only if the payment has not been received within how many days of the due date, and the fee is capped at the LESSER of $50 or what percentage of the monthly rent?
choice_a: Three days; ten percent of the monthly rent
choice_b: Ten days; five percent of the monthly rent
choice_c: Five days; five percent of the monthly rent
choice_d: Five days; ten percent of the monthly rent
explanation: RPL 238-a bars a late fee unless rent remains unpaid five days after the due date, and caps any late fee at the lesser of $50 or 5% of the monthly rent -- whichever amount is smaller.
source_note: NY source: RPL 238-a (HSTPA 2019) -- late fee timing trigger and dollar/percentage cap

question: A tenant's rent of $2,000 is due on the 1st of the month and is paid in full on the 4th of the month. Under RPL 238-a (HSTPA 2019), may the landlord charge a late fee?
choice_a: Yes -- $50, since any late payment triggers the cap amount
choice_b: Yes -- 5% of $2,000, since the payment was after the due date
choice_c: Yes, but only if the lease is silent on late fees
choice_d: No -- a late fee cannot be charged unless rent remains unpaid five days after the due date
explanation: Because RPL 238-a prohibits a late fee unless rent is unpaid for at least five days after its due date, and this tenant paid on day 4 (within the five-day grace period), no late fee may be charged.
source_note: NY source: RPL 238-a (HSTPA 2019) -- applied scenario, payment within 5-day grace period

question: Under RPL 238-a (HSTPA 2019), a landlord may charge a prospective residential tenant a fee for a background and credit check, but the fee is capped at the LESSER of the actual cost of the check or:
choice_a: Twenty dollars
choice_b: Fifty dollars
choice_c: One hundred dollars
choice_d: One percent of the annual rent
explanation: RPL 238-a caps a landlord's application/background-check fee at the lesser of the actual cost of the background and credit check or $20, and generally bars separate application-processing fees.
source_note: NY source: RPL 238-a (HSTPA 2019) -- application/background check fee cap of $20 or actual cost

question: Under RPL 238-a (HSTPA 2019), if a rental applicant provides the landlord with a copy of the applicant's own background and credit check completed within the preceding 30 days, the landlord must:
choice_a: Still charge the full $20 fee regardless of the applicant's own report
choice_b: Waive any separate background/credit check fee
choice_c: Charge double the standard fee to verify the applicant's report
choice_d: Reject the applicant's own report and require a new one at the applicant's expense
explanation: RPL 238-a requires a landlord to waive the background/credit check fee where the applicant furnishes the applicant's own qualifying background and credit check obtained within the prior 30 days.
source_note: NY source: RPL 238-a (HSTPA 2019) -- fee waiver for applicant-supplied recent background check

question: Under RPL 238-a (HSTPA 2019), a landlord who charges a rental applicant a background/credit check fee must also provide the applicant with:
choice_a: A written promise to rent the unit to the applicant if the check is favorable
choice_b: A refund of the fee within 90 days regardless of the outcome
choice_c: A copy of the background/credit check results and the receipt or invoice from the company performing the check
choice_d: Nothing further -- the fee itself satisfies the statute
explanation: RPL 238-a conditions a landlord's right to collect a background/credit check fee on providing the applicant a copy of the check results along with the receipt or invoice documenting the fee charged by the screening company.
source_note: NY source: RPL 238-a (HSTPA 2019) -- disclosure obligations tied to charging an application fee

question: Under RPAPL Section 711(2), as amended by the HSTPA in 2019, before a landlord may commence a nonpayment eviction proceeding, the landlord must first serve the tenant with a written rent demand giving the tenant AT LEAST how much notice?
choice_a: Three days
choice_b: Five days
choice_c: Seven days
choice_d: Fourteen days
explanation: RPAPL 711(2), as amended by the HSTPA, requires a written rent demand giving the tenant at least fourteen days' notice before a nonpayment proceeding may be commenced -- a substantial lengthening of the pre-HSTPA notice period commonly reported as three days.
source_note: hedge: current 14-day figure independently verified via live fetch of nysenate.gov RPAPL 711; the pre-HSTPA baseline of 3 days reflects widely-reported secondary sources and was not independently re-verified against pre-2019 statutory text. NY source: RPAPL 711(2) (HSTPA 2019)

question: Under RPAPL Section 732, as amended by the HSTPA in 2019, once a summary nonpayment proceeding is commenced, the notice of petition must be returnable -- that is, the tenant must have a hearing date -- no sooner than how many days after service?
choice_a: Ten days
choice_b: Five days
choice_c: Three days
choice_d: Thirty days
explanation: RPAPL 732 requires the notice of petition to be returnable at least ten days after service, giving the tenant a minimum window to prepare a defense before the initial court date -- longer than the pre-HSTPA period commonly reported as five days.
source_note: hedge: current 10-day figure independently verified via live fetch of nysenate.gov RPAPL 732; the pre-HSTPA baseline of 5 days reflects widely-reported secondary sources and was not independently re-verified against pre-2019 statutory text. NY source: RPAPL 732 (HSTPA 2019)

question: Under RPAPL Section 749(2)(a), as amended by the HSTPA in 2019, once a warrant of eviction has been issued, the marshal or sheriff must give the tenant written notice of AT LEAST how many days before physically executing the warrant and removing the tenant?
choice_a: Seventy-two hours
choice_b: Fourteen days
choice_c: Three days
choice_d: Thirty days
explanation: RPAPL 749(2)(a) requires at least fourteen days' written notice before execution of a warrant of eviction, substantially longer than the pre-HSTPA period commonly reported as 72 hours -- giving tenants more time to relocate or seek emergency relief.
source_note: hedge: current 14-day figure independently verified via live fetch of nysenate.gov RPAPL 749; the pre-HSTPA baseline of 72 hours reflects widely-reported secondary sources and was not independently re-verified against pre-2019 statutory text. NY source: RPAPL 749(2)(a) (HSTPA 2019)

question: Under RPAPL Section 702, in a residential nonpayment proceeding, the amount a landlord may seek is limited to "rent" as statutorily defined, meaning the landlord generally may NOT include in the nonpayment claim:
choice_a: The monthly amount charged for use and occupancy of the dwelling
choice_b: Rent that has actually accrued and remains unpaid
choice_c: Late fees, legal fees, or other charges the lease labels as "additional rent"
choice_d: Amounts due under a written or oral rental agreement for occupancy of the unit
explanation: RPAPL 702 defines "rent" in a residential nonpayment proceeding as the periodic amount charged for use and occupation of the dwelling, and bars landlords from bootstrapping late fees, legal fees, or other charges into a nonpayment claim merely by labeling them "additional rent" in the lease.
source_note: NY source: RPAPL 702 -- definition of "rent" limits nonpayment proceeding claims to rent itself

question: Under RPAPL Section 853, a landlord who removes a residential tenant from possession through forcible or unlawful means -- such as changing the locks or shutting off utilities without a court-ordered warrant of eviction -- exposes the landlord to:
choice_a: No civil liability, since eviction is a landlord's right
choice_b: Liability limited to a single month's rent
choice_c: Criminal liability only, with no civil remedy available to the tenant
choice_d: Treble (triple) damages in a civil action brought by the tenant
explanation: RPAPL 853 allows a tenant who has been forcibly or unlawfully removed from possession to sue for treble (three times) damages, reflecting New York's strong policy against self-help evictions -- a landlord must obtain a court judgment and warrant of eviction before removing a tenant.
source_note: NY source: RPAPL 853 -- treble damages for forcible or unlawful eviction; self-help eviction prohibited

question: A landlord, frustrated that a residential tenant has stopped paying rent, changes the locks on the apartment door while the tenant is at work and refuses to let the tenant back in, without ever going to court. Under New York law, this is:
choice_a: An illegal self-help eviction that exposes the landlord to treble damages under RPAPL 853
choice_b: A lawful remedy available to any landlord once rent is 30 days overdue
choice_c: Lawful only if the landlord first sends a 3-day notice
choice_d: Lawful, provided the landlord returns the tenant's belongings within 24 hours
explanation: New York prohibits self-help evictions entirely -- a landlord must obtain a court judgment and warrant of eviction, executed by a marshal or sheriff, before removing a tenant. Changing the locks without a court order is an illegal eviction exposing the landlord to treble damages under RPAPL 853.
source_note: NY source: RPAPL 853 -- applied scenario, illegal lockout

question: Under RPL Section 223-b, a landlord's service of a notice to quit, commencement of an eviction proceeding, or attempt to substantially alter lease terms is presumed retaliatory if it occurs within one year after the tenant:
choice_a: Referred a new tenant to the landlord for a vacant unit
choice_b: Made a good-faith complaint to the landlord or a government authority about a health or safety violation
choice_c: Requested a change in the color of the apartment's paint
choice_d: Paid rent more than five days early for three consecutive months
explanation: RPL 223-b creates a rebuttable one-year presumption of retaliation when a landlord takes adverse action against a tenant after the tenant makes a good-faith complaint about a health or safety violation, seeks to enforce habitability rights, or has previously won a related dispute against the same landlord.
source_note: NY source: RPL 223-b -- retaliatory eviction presumption trigger

question: Under RPL 223-b, once the one-year presumption of retaliatory eviction is triggered, the landlord may still prevail by:
choice_a: Simply denying the allegation without offering any evidence
choice_b: Showing that the tenant has since paid all rent owed, which automatically rebuts the presumption
choice_c: Proving a legitimate, non-retaliatory motive for the action by a preponderance of the evidence
choice_d: Waiting out the one-year period before taking any action, which is the only available defense
explanation: The RPL 223-b presumption of retaliation is rebuttable -- the landlord can overcome it by proving, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the action was taken for a legitimate, non-retaliatory business reason unrelated to the tenant's complaint or rights-enforcement activity.
source_note: NY source: RPL 223-b -- rebuttable presumption, landlord's burden of proof

question: Under RPL Section 235-b, the implied warranty of habitability in a residential lease requires that the premises, and the common areas used by the tenant, be:
choice_a: Renovated with new appliances at least once every five years
choice_b: Maintained at the tenant's expense unless otherwise stated in the lease
choice_c: Inspected annually by a licensed real estate broker
choice_d: Fit for human habitation and free from conditions dangerous to life, health, or safety
explanation: RPL 235-b implies, in every written or oral residential lease, a covenant that the premises and areas used in connection with the premises (such as common areas) are fit for human habitation and for the uses reasonably intended, and free of conditions dangerous to life, health, or safety.
source_note: NY source: RPL 235-b -- implied warranty of habitability

question: Under RPL 235-b, may a residential landlord and tenant agree in the lease to waive the tenant's rights under the implied warranty of habitability?
choice_a: No -- any lease provision purporting to waive the warranty of habitability is void as against public policy
choice_b: Yes, if the tenant is a licensed real estate agent
choice_c: Yes, if the landlord provides a rent discount in exchange
choice_d: Yes, but only for leases longer than two years
explanation: RPL 235-b expressly provides that any agreement waiving or modifying the warranty of habitability is void as contrary to public policy -- the protection cannot be bargained away regardless of consideration offered.
source_note: NY source: RPL 235-b -- non-waivability of the warranty of habitability

question: Under RPL Section 234, if a residential lease gives the landlord the right to recover attorneys' fees from the tenant when the tenant breaches the lease, the statute:
choice_a: Voids the landlord's attorneys' fee provision entirely, leaving neither party able to recover fees
choice_b: Implies a reciprocal covenant requiring the landlord to pay the tenant's reasonable attorneys' fees if the landlord breaches or the tenant successfully defends
choice_c: Allows the landlord to recover fees but caps them at $500
choice_d: Applies only to commercial leases, not residential leases
explanation: RPL 234 implies a reciprocal covenant in residential leases: if the lease allows the landlord to recover attorneys' fees from the tenant for the tenant's breach, the law automatically implies an equivalent covenant requiring the landlord to pay the tenant's reasonable attorneys' fees for the landlord's own breach or a successful tenant defense.
source_note: NY source: RPL 234 -- reciprocal attorneys' fees covenant in residential leases

question: Under RPL 234, may a landlord recover attorneys' fees from a residential tenant based solely on a default judgment (where the tenant never appeared to contest the proceeding)?
choice_a: Yes, as long as the lease authorizes it
choice_b: Yes, but only in proceedings filed in New York City
choice_c: No -- RPL 234 bars recovery of attorneys' fees against a tenant on a default judgment
choice_d: Yes, provided the fees do not exceed one month's rent
explanation: RPL 234 specifically prohibits a landlord from recovering attorneys' fees against a residential tenant where the landlord's award would rest on a default judgment, since the tenant never had the opportunity to contest the underlying claim -- an exception exists for certain cooperative proprietary leases.
source_note: NY source: RPL 234 -- bar on attorneys' fee recovery via default judgment

question: A landlord and tenant sign a residential lease containing a clause stating the tenant "waives any right to attorneys' fees from the landlord under any circumstance." Under RPL 234, this waiver clause is:
choice_a: Enforceable exactly as written, since parties may freely contract around RPL 234
choice_b: Enforceable only if a licensed attorney reviewed the lease before signing
choice_c: Enforceable, but only for leases under one year
choice_d: Void, because RPL 234's reciprocal fee-shifting protection cannot be waived as a matter of public policy
explanation: RPL 234 declares any attempt to waive its reciprocal attorneys' fee protections void as contrary to public policy, meaning a lease clause purporting to waive the tenant's reciprocal fee-shifting rights has no legal effect.
source_note: NY source: RPL 234 -- waiver of reciprocal fee-shifting protection is void

question: Which of the following residential rental arrangements is generally EXEMPT from the one-month security deposit cap under GOL 7-108 (HSTPA 2019)?
choice_a: A seasonal vacation rental meeting the statute's seasonal-use criteria
choice_b: A standard year-to-year lease in a market-rate apartment building
choice_c: A month-to-month tenancy in a non-rent-stabilized apartment
choice_d: A two-year lease in a market-rate apartment building
explanation: GOL 7-108's one-month deposit cap applies broadly to non-rent-stabilized residential units, but the statute carves out narrow exceptions, including certain seasonal-use rentals and owner-occupied cooperative units, which are not subject to the flat one-month limit.
source_note: NY source: General Obligations Law Section 7-108 (HSTPA 2019) -- statutory exceptions to the deposit cap

question: A tenant vacates an apartment on June 1. The landlord finally sends an itemized statement of deposit deductions on June 25 -- 24 days later. Under GOL 7-108 (HSTPA 2019), what is the legal consequence of this delay?
choice_a: There is no consequence, since 24 days is a reasonable amount of time
choice_b: The landlord forfeits the right to retain any part of the security deposit, since the statement was not sent within 14 days
choice_c: The landlord may still deduct for damages but must pay the tenant a $50 penalty
choice_d: The tenant must sue within 10 days or lose the right to challenge the deductions
explanation: Because GOL 7-108 requires the itemized statement within 14 days after the tenant vacates, and the landlord here took 24 days, the landlord forfeits the right to retain any portion of the deposit regardless of whether legitimate deductions existed.
source_note: NY source: General Obligations Law Section 7-108(2)(a) (HSTPA 2019) -- applied scenario, missed 14-day deadline

question: Which New York statute, added by the HSTPA in 2019, directly caps the amount a residential landlord may charge as a security deposit, as distinct from the pre-existing statute (GOL 7-103) governing a broker's or landlord's trust-fund handling of a deposit already collected?
choice_a: General Obligations Law Section 7-103
choice_b: RPL Section 443
choice_c: General Obligations Law Section 7-108
choice_d: 19 NYCRR 175.3(b)
explanation: GOL 7-108, added by the HSTPA in 2019, sets the substantive cap and procedural rules for residential security deposits (amount, itemization, timing). GOL 7-103 is the older trust-fund statute governing how a deposit, once collected, must be held and accounted for -- the two statutes work together but address different aspects of deposit handling.
source_note: NY source: General Obligations Law Section 7-108 (HSTPA 2019) vs. Section 7-103 -- distinguishing deposit cap from trust-fund handling
